note: Evidence cards for the Climate tab. 'measured' is what the laboratory or field actually measured; 'inferred' is the environmental condition the authors reconstruct from it. Summaries are this site's own wording; consult the original paper before citing.

studies.title: Oxygen isotopes in orangutan teeth reveal recent and ancient climate variation
studies.citation: Smith, T. M. et al. (2024). eLife 12: RP90217.
studies.archive: Biological archive: museum and cave-fossil teeth
studies.question: Can oxygen isotopes in orangutan tooth enamel record rainfall seasonality, and how did Pleistocene and early-Holocene conditions on Sumatra and Borneo compare with the recent past?
studies.location: Sumatra (Lida Ajer and Sibrambang caves) and Borneo (Niah Caves); modern museum specimens from Borneo and Sumatra
studies.scope: Local to regional (individual animals' home ranges); not a basin-wide or global signal
studies.period: Modern specimens collected c. 1880s–1939; fossils with minimum U-series ages of about 8–9 ka (Niah), 33–40 ka (Lida Ajer) and 60–70 ka (Sibrambang)
studies.dating: Uranium-series minimum ages for fossils (ka = thousand years before present); collection dates for museum specimens
studies.evidence: 12 molars from 6 modern orangutans (2,016 measurements) and 6 fossil molars (955 measurements)
studies.measured: δ18O of enamel, by ion microprobe (SHRIMP SI) in ~15×20 µm spots along daily growth increments
studies.inferred: Rainfall seasonality and relative wetness or dryness (via the isotopic composition of drinking water and food)
studies.resolution: About weekly within each animal's tooth-forming years (roughly 3–11 years per individual)
studies.finding: Modern Sumatran teeth show clear annual or twice-yearly cycles; Bornean teeth are less regular, with swings that may reflect El Niño years. Fossil Sumatran teeth resemble modern ones; fossil Bornean teeth from Niah are at least 2‰ heavier, which the authors read as possibly drier conditions with weaker monsoon rainfall.
studies.uncertainty: Small sample (6 modern, 6 fossil molars); fossil ages are minimum estimates; no local rainfall-isotope measurements, so modelled precipitation isotopes were used; diet, canopy height and altitude can also shift enamel δ18O. Enamel isotopes are not a thermometer and do not give rainfall amounts directly.
studies.data: Source data in the article's supplementary files

studies.title: brGDGT temperature reconstruction from interior Alaska: assessing 14,000 years of deglacial to Holocene temperature variability and potential effects on early human settlement
studies.citation: Kielhofer, J. R. et al. (2023). Quaternary Science Reviews, article 107979.
studies.archive: Archaeological sites: buried soils at occupation sites
studies.question: What were temperatures like when people first settled the Tanana Valley, and did temperature change drive changes in occupation?
studies.location: Middle Tanana Valley, interior Alaska, including the Keystone Dune site
studies.scope: Local (valley); the authors stress that it did not follow the expected global pattern
studies.period: About 14,000 years ago to the present (deglacial to Holocene)
studies.dating: Radiocarbon-based site chronologies (calibrated years before present); see the paper for the age model
studies.evidence: Sediment and soil samples from archaeological sites
studies.measured: Branched GDGTs: membrane lipids of soil bacteria, whose molecular structure varies with temperature
studies.resolution: Multi-centennial to millennial: each sample integrates a soil horizon (see the paper for sample spacing)
studies.finding: Temperatures stayed fairly stable through the record, contrary to expectations of large deglacial swings, so temperature alone does not explain changes in human occupation; relative warmth may have made the valley attractive.
studies.uncertainty: Calibration error of about ±2.8 °C on each estimate; soils integrate long periods; brGDGT temperature relationships vary between environments; aridity was not reconstructed.

studies.title: Orbital and millennial Antarctic climate variability over the past 800,000 years
studies.question: How did Antarctic temperature vary through the last eight glacial cycles?
studies.scope: Site to regional (East Antarctic plateau), not global mean temperature
studies.period: About 800,000 years ago to the present
studies.dating: EDC3 age model (glaciological model with tie points); ages in years before 1950
studies.evidence: 3,259.7 m of ice, sampled in 55 cm sections (about 5,800 samples)
studies.measured: Deuterium content of the ice (δD, ±0.5‰ analytical accuracy)
studies.inferred: Local temperature relative to the last 1,000 years, after corrections for seawater isotopic composition and ice-sheet elevation
studies.resolution: Decades near the top to more than a thousand years per sample near the bottom
studies.finding: Eight glacial–interglacial cycles, with Dome C temperature ranging from about 10.6 °C below to 5.5 °C above the average of the last 1,000 years; interglacials differ in warmth, which the authors link to the interplay of Earth's orbital cycles.
studies.uncertainty: The isotope–temperature relationship can change with moisture source and snowfall seasonality; age-model uncertainty grows with depth; a single site is not a global average.
studies.data: NOAA/World Data Service for Paleoclimatology, contribution 2007-091

studies.title: Holocene global mean surface temperature, a multi-method reconstruction approach
studies.citation: Kaufman, D. et al. (2020). Scientific Data 7: 201.
studies.question: How did global and latitude-band mean surface temperature change over the last 12,000 years, with realistic uncertainty?
studies.period: 12,000 years before present (1950 CE) to the 20th century
studies.dating: Proxy chronologies from the source records; 100-year bins centred on each age
studies.evidence: Temperature 12k Database v1.0 (lake and marine sediments, pollen, ice cores and other proxies)
studies.measured: Many proxy types, each already calibrated to temperature in the source studies
studies.inferred: Annual mean surface temperature anomaly relative to 1800–1900 CE
studies.finding: The warmest 200-year interval was around 6,500 years ago, about 0.7 °C (0.4 to 1.8) warmer than the 19th century; temperature then cooled by about 0.08 °C per 1,000 years until the industrial era.
studies.uncertainty: Five statistical methods × 500 ensemble members; the 5th–95th percentile range includes proxy, chronology and method uncertainty. Centennial bins cannot resolve decades, and proxies are uneven in space and season. Some studies argue the early-Holocene warmth reflects summer-biased proxies (the 'Holocene temperature conundrum').
